articles.headline: D.C. Circuit Lets Pentagon Blacklist Anthropic Claude
articles.deck: A 2-1 majority says refusal to enable military functions meets the procurement law definition of supply-chain risk.

pullquote.text: As Anthropic admits, the company encodes restrictions into Claude that prevent the model from performing tasks that Anthropic wishes to prevent.

body: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld the Pentagon blacklist of Anthropic in a 2-1 decision. The court found the Defense Department could designate Claude a supply-chain risk under federal procurement law after the company refused to permit military uses. The ruling leaves the ban in place while a conflicting California decision remains under appeal.

The majority said the law covers denial of function, not only sabotage by adversaries. It held that Anthropic disabling features sought by the Defense Department fit the definition in section 4713. The opinion stated “case raises profoundly difficult questions about the appropriate military uses of an almost unimaginably powerful new technology.” The court added Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “must determine how best to balance the competing risks,” and found no breach of authority.

The dissent by Judge Karen Henderson said the statute targets infiltration of federal systems by hostile actors, not open enforcement of use limits. A judge in the Northern District of California had rejected the designation under section 3252, which requires bad motive by an adversary. The appeals court said it had exclusive authority under the broader procurement provision. It left that California order intact while upholding the second designation.

Anthropic sued in March after federal agencies were ordered to stop using its products and defense contractors were barred from business with the company. The same panel denied emergency relief in April. The company may seek full court review or petition the Supreme Court. Alternatives named for replacing Claude include Grok, Gemini and GPT models. Some employees at Google and OpenAI objected on ethical grounds. The companies described support for the government as crucial. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the administration and company are “in tune.” Sales have grown as a public offering remains expected.

art.caption: The exterior facade of the Pentagon on a clear day. The court left in place the Defense Department ban on Anthropic technology.

articles.headline: MIT tool flags suicide risk in crisis texts
articles.deck: The system searches counselor conversations for phrases tied to 49 established risk factors.

pullquote.text: We wanted to know what type of symptoms predict the highest suicide risk,

body: MIT scientists built a language-processing tool that estimates suicide risk from text messages exchanged with crisis counselors. The system searches messages for phrases linked to 49 established risk factors and assigns weights to predict severity. Researchers report that the tool accurately predicted risk in new conversations it had not seen.

The tool was developed by Daniel Low, a former graduate student in Senior Research Scientist Satra Ghosh’s Senseable Intelligence Group who is now a research scientist at the Child Mind Institute. The team built a lexicon with about 60 words or phrases for each risk factor, with relevance confirmed by expert clinicians. They trained a machine learning model on de-identified texts from approximately 16,000 conversations with Crisis Text Line volunteer counselors.

Crisis Text Line assessments grouped the conversations into three risk levels: non-suicidal, suicidal ideation without imminent risk, and imminent risk. The imminent risk group included people with a plan for suicide or intent to die within the next 48 hours. “We wanted to know what type of symptoms predict the highest suicide risk,” Low says. The researchers sought patterns visible during a crisis rather than recalled afterward in surveys.

The model found that mentions of lethal means and substance use were more likely to be expressed by the highest-risk group than depressed mood or fatigue. Expressions of active suicidal ideation and self-injury were also strong predictors. Intermediate predictors included anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, and emotional pain. The model assigns a weight to each factor based on its contribution to risk. Terms related to hopelessness contributed to a lesser degree.

Low stresses that the prediction model is a simpler lightweight model that can run on a personal computer. Unlike large language models, it requires less computational power and reduces cost and privacy concerns. It is interpretable and flags words of concern so users understand the basis for each assessment. The researchers note that lexicons do not consider context and can miss similar terms not explicitly included. They often use the lexicon in parallel to guarantee flagging certain terms and to maintain data privacy.

The researchers report their results in the Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science. The tool is already helping clarify which risk factors matter most in times of crisis. With more validation, it could help with risk assessment in clinical settings and crisis-support situations. Suicide attempts remain difficult to predict, even for trained clinicians. The model does not replace judgment. It sorts signals. The final decision remains with trained human counselors.

articles.headline: $10 Million Funds 50 Psychiatric Research Fellowships
articles.deck: Five two-year awards for graduate students and postdocs will be made each year for a decade.

pullquote.text: Pat and Jim have remained steadfast in their decades-long commitment to bold research that can transform mental wellness,

body: Patricia and James Poitras have committed $10 million to create 50 two-year fellowships for MIT graduate students and postdocs studying major mental illness. The program will award five fellowships each year for the next decade through the Poitras Center for Psychiatric Disorders Research at the McGovern Institute for Brain Research. The gift targets early career scientists focused specifically on psychiatric disorders.

The $10 million gift addresses severe depression and anxiety, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and other complex psychiatric conditions. It extends Poitras family support for mental health research at MIT to over $100 million. The investment focuses on PhD students and postdocs at a time when federal funding has grown especially precarious. Five McGovern Institute researchers have been selected as the inaugural cohort of fellows and scholars.

The inaugural cohort includes Amrita Lamba, Linghua Zhang, Hoonwon Lee, Smriti Saini and Karen Pang. Their projects span multiple areas of brain research and could reveal new ways to heal the mind. The next application window for Poitras Center fellowships will open in May 2027. Robert Desimone directs the McGovern Institute and heads the Poitras Center. James Poitras chairs the board of the McGovern Institute.

In 2007 the Poitras family gave $20 million to launch the Poitras Center. The center bridges basic neuroscience, clinical psychiatry and molecular biology to study psychiatric disorders from molecular mechanisms to whole brain systems and guide novel therapies. Later investments supported work from genome engineering to cognitive neuroscience, including how ketamine acts on synaptic communication and why schizophrenia distorts inner speech and reasoning. Advances include an AI powered calculator for predicting bipolar disorder risk in adolescents, molecular carriers for delivering therapies, and strategies using brain activity patterns to match patients with treatments. Patricia and James Poitras envisioned a future for solving enigmatic mental conditions.

articles.headline: AI tutoring matches human tutoring on GRE
articles.deck: StudentBench trial of 2,383 learners reports equivalent gains at a fraction of cost.
body: StudentBench compared AI tutoring with expert human tutoring across 2,383 participants answering Quantitative and Verbal GRE questions. AI tutoring was statistically equivalent to expert human tutoring for GRE learning gains. The comparison used more than 175,000 student-AI messages to study whether large language models produce learning gains equivalent to human tutoring. Participants received AI tutoring, human tutoring, or no tutoring.

The best performing AI tutor surpassed the human tutor on average in five of the seven GRE domains. Statistical equivalence for overall GRE learning gains reached p equals .015. A second study asked expert human tutors to compare lesson plans and practice problems generated by large language models. The comparison used 2,028 pairwise rubric evaluations. Together the two studies separate AI tutors across lesson planning, practice-problem creation, conversational pedagogy, cost and engagement.

One AI tutor achieved learning gains equivalent to human tutoring at 918 times lower cost. Equivalence in that comparison reached p equals .044. Cost per percentage point gained was USD 0.0052 for AI versus USD 4.81 for human. For Quantitative GRE sessions faster AI replies correlated with more student messages. More student messages correlated with more correct practice. More correct practice correlated with larger learning gains. All three correlations were reported at p .002. The StudentBench platform is freely available at https://studentbench.org. The measure is gain on test questions. The difference is price, not proof of understanding. The test counts answers, not comprehension.

articles.headline: Small brain zone sustains fear after amygdala burst
articles.deck: Researchers link continuous defensive behavior in mice to Drd2-positive neurons in the amygdalostriatal transition zone.

pullquote.text: The neural and behavioral results that we observed were striking,

body: A Neuron study identifies the amygdalostriatal transition zone as the structure that sustains defensive behavior after brief threat signals from the amygdala fade. The work was led by Fergil Mills at the University of Utah with Kay M. Tye at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies. Experiments in mice show neurons in the small zone fire for the full duration of a threat cue. The finding bridges learning about danger and maintaining a defensive state.

The question centers on timing. A 1995 study of rats showed fear learning neurons in the amygdala respond to threat sounds in a brief rapid burst lasting only milliseconds. A 2002 laboratory study showed warning signals travel rapidly from the amygdala directly into the neighboring zone. A 2009 study of rodents described the puzzle that amygdala signals fade almost immediately even though defensive behaviors persist for tens of seconds.

The team first examined genetic identity. They extracted and analyzed the genetic material of 97,434 individual cell nuclei from the brains of mice. The analysis indicated the zone has a distinct genetic identity. It contains an unusually high concentration of Drd2 positive neurons which carry a receptor for dopamine. About 71 percent of the neurons were of this type compared to just 26 percent for Drd1a positive neurons.

The team then measured electrical activity in 15 live mice. The mice were trained where a 20 second auditory tone predicted a mild foot shock while a different 20 second tone predicted a sweet liquid reward. Neurons in the zone responded strongly to the shock predicting tone. Unlike brief bursts in the amygdala the neurons fired continuously for the entire 20 second duration of the threat cue. Trials with the highest freezing showed firing rates over three times higher than trials with low defensive behavior.

The researchers tested causation with optogenetics which allows control of specific neurons using light. They tested 18 mice engineered so neurons in the zone could be activated by blue light lasers. Light delivery caused the mice to freeze immediately. In a separate test where one side of an enclosure triggered the laser the mice avoided that side. Tests in 35 additional mice isolated cell types. Activating only Drd2 positive neurons produced freezing and avoidance while activating Drd1a positive neurons had no effect on these behaviors. A rotating rod test showed freezing was defensive not a general inability to move.

Calcium imaging tracked the cell types during the tone task using miniature microscopes attached to the heads of 15 mice. Calcium levels rise when neurons are active. Drd2 positive neurons maintained high sustained activity throughout the threat predicting tones. The team then silenced Drd2 positive neurons in 21 mice with a different optogenetic tool. Blocking these neurons reduced defensive behaviors such as freezing or sudden darting by nearly 50 percent. Blocking did not change responses to reward cues nor general movement in an open arena.

The experiments used a single foot shock threat and a single sweet drink reward. The zone responded to specific warning tones not fear associated contexts. The authors view the circuit as complementary to amygdala learning circuits.

articles.headline: EFF says EU Kids Act mandates intrusive age checks
articles.deck: The proposal would phase youth access by age and make safety the default, with verification for adults.

pullquote.text: it will put online services behind age gates, expand the use of intrusive age verification, and undermine the privacy of all users.

body: The Electronic Frontier Foundation says the EU Commission draft EU Kids Act would place online services behind age gates and require intrusive verification. The group says the measure would expand checks across mainstream platforms and reduce privacy for adults as well as minors. The proposal sets phased access rules for social media and video sharing.

The draft creates three tiers. There are no service accounts for children under 13. Accounts for users from 13 to 15 require tight parental supervision. Users from 15 to 18 receive autonomous accounts in a safe by design environment. Full access is reserved for adults. Parents must set up accounts and prove parental status. Checks rely on the EU age verification scheme. Providers may skip verification for existing accounts only with a high degree of confidence the user is above the threshold.

The second pillar is safety by design. It covers social media, video sharing, online games, AI companions, chatbots and app stores. Providers must make child safe design the default and may relax rules only after age assurance shows the user is an adult. Rules address infinite scrolling, account settings and choice over recommender systems. AI services must reduce exposure to emotional dependency and harmful interaction. Games must include contact protections. App stores act as gatekeepers through age ratings.

The Foundation argues age gates undermine civil liberties and reduce safety. It says barriers fall hardest on marginalized groups and create infrastructure for control. It says the rules entrench large technology firms. Small and medium sized enterprises receive no exemption while nonprofit encyclopedias, scientific repositories, educational services and open source platforms are exempt. Most firms will adopt strict checks to limit legal risk. Critics say the design rules don’t fit decentralized networks such as the Fediverse—where central enforcement is difficult.

The proposal avoids a blanket social media ban. A French court declared undifferentiated bans unconstitutional. The draft distinguishes age groups and services under a risk based approach. The Foundation says thresholds remain a blunt proxy for maturity. It says the focus on safety neglects privacy, freedom of expression and the right of children to access information and participate online. The draft lacked a full impact assessment. The Foundation urges EU lawmakers to remove the most harmful provisions and protect fundamental rights for all users now.

articles.headline: PrismML Shrinks Model for Smart Glasses
articles.deck: 2-billion-parameter Bonsai version runs locally on Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 Platform.
body: PrismML has created a version of its tiny language models for smart glasses running on Qualcomm Snapdragon chips. The 1-bit Bonsai LLM runs locally on AI smart glasses built on the Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 Platform. The model was showcased at the Snapdragon Summit. It contains 2-billion parameters tuned for vision and language. It is shrunk by 4x from a larger model. Wearers can ask what they are looking at in real time.

The lab was founded by Caltech researchers and is advised by Ion Stoica of UC Berkeley. Its method shrinks larger models substantially while retaining almost all of their performance on standard benchmarks. The approach targets open-weight AI that runs on devices. It aims to make better use of the computing power they already have. The startup presents local execution as an alternative to dependence on proprietary AI labs.

The startup pitches this approach as an alternative to depending on the privacy promises of proprietary AI labs and their insatiable need for more compute. Releasing a model for the Qualcomm chip is a step toward that vision. No smart glasses running PrismML have been announced yet. The Summit demonstration focused on local vision and language use on glasses hardware. The model handles questions about visible objects in real time. Compact size preserves benchmark performance for practical deployment on existing chips. The goal is open-weight AI on devices with better use of available power. The method reduces model size while keeping capability. The result fits eyewear constraints and supports everyday questions.

articles.headline: Umpires shift zone toward automated system in 2026
articles.deck: Analysis of 4,114,256 pitches and 8,447 challenges finds temporary adjustment after overturns and many overturnable calls left unchallenged.
body: The effective strike zone called by Major League Baseball umpires moved toward the automated zone in 2026. The finding comes from 4,114,256 called pitches from 2015 through 2026 and 8,447 challenges from the 2026 season. Umpires make every ball and strike call under the Automated Ball-Strike challenge system. Players can ask the automated system to publicly overturn those decisions. The shift exceeded the trajectory observed in prior seasons. Consistency largely continued its existing trend.

The analysis tracks where umpires placed the effective strike zone boundary and how consistently they applied that boundary. The work studies umpire judgment and player behavior under algorithmic review. The setting is distinctive. Following an overturned call, umpires temporarily adjusted subsequent decisions near the corrected boundary. Those effects didn’t consistently persist into the next game. The adjustment was local and short lived. The result was correction without a lasting reset.

Count dependent variation in calling remained. Differences associated with player status narrowed. Players left many overturnable calls unchallenged. Challenge decisions appeared to rest more strongly on immediately observable evidence than on the precise geometry of the automated zone. The study examines which calls players chose to challenge. Players selected a subset of calls for review. Selective review corrects individual errors. It also reshapes judgment, adaptation and strategic behavior.

The 2026 system kept the initial call with the umpire. Players selected a subset of calls for automated review and public overturn. The effective boundary shifted toward the automated zone. Adjustment after correction was temporary. Many overturnable calls went unchallenged. Count variation remained. Player status differences narrowed. The hand made the call. The system checked the edge. The eye adjusted. The review remained selective. That is how a boundary moves under review.

articles.headline: Meta steers Muse toward glasses after launches
articles.deck: Anthropic released Opus 5.5 90 minutes before OpenAI updated GPT-6, while Muse is reportedly ahead of early ChatGPT numbers.
body: Anthropic released Opus 5.5. OpenAI followed with GPT-6 updates 90 minutes later. Meta took attention with Muse, its personal agent. The agent is reportedly outpacing ChatGPT early numbers. It is headed to smart glasses and a tiny Tamagotchi-style device next. The order of releases framed the week. A consumer product drew the focus. The gap was narrow. The timing was tight. Model drops came in sequence. Muse sits apart from those drops. It is described as a personal agent. That distinction matters.

On TechCrunch Equity, Kirsten Korosec, Anthony Ha and Sean O’Kane examined Meta consumer AI strategy. They traced where money is flowing. They assessed what it means for startups building on top of this technology. They asked which AI products might become part of people daily lives. The discussion centered on product distribution. Glasses and small devices change placement. Placement changes use. Startups face a platform question. Build above Muse or compete with it. Money follows access to users. Access follows daily habit. Habit forms around concrete tasks. Tasks decide retention.

They also addressed a16z new school for aspiring founders. They covered two very different AI and hardware deals. The items share a theme. Founders need routes to users. Labs need outlets for models. The contest is not only benchmarks. It is daily habit. Schools for founders address supply. Deals for hardware address demand. Both point to deployment. Models improve in labs. Products win through repeated use. The record so far is early numbers. Early numbers don’t settle use. Not yet.

boxes.title: The Pentagon Blacklist Stands
paras: Courts let the Pentagon blacklist a model maker. A US appeals court approved the Department of Defense’s blacklisting of Anthropic technology after the company withheld certain AI features from the military.

In a 2-1 ruling, the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit said the Trump administration had authority to blacklist Anthropic even if Anthropic had no malicious intent. The department had ample support for its conclusion that the continued integration of Claude into the department’s information systems presented a statutorily covered national-security risk.

Anthropic encodes restrictions into Claude that prevent the model from performing tasks. The panel said the case raises profoundly difficult questions about the appropriate military uses of an almost unimaginably powerful new technology. Judges refused to second-guess the Trump administration.
